articles.title: New right to bereavement leave to cover step and half relatives
articles.summary: The new law will also cover foster, kinship care and adoptive relationships, as well as early pregnancy loss.
articles.content:
Following a consultation, the government has now set out exactly who the new right will apply to.

It said including step, half, adoptive, foster and kinship care relationships – where family or friends take care of a child when their parents are not able to - would "bring the UK's laws into the 21st century".

Welcoming the move, the chief executive of the Kinship charity, Lucy Peake, said: "Kinship families grieve the loss of a loved one just like any other family, and this right to take time off work will help ensure they are treated fairly alongside other bereaved families."

Meanwhile, the right also covers women and their partners who experience a pregnancy loss, including miscarriage, terminations and unsuccessful IVF embryo transfers.

It will also apply to the other biological parent, or intended parents in a surrogacy arrangement.

Employees will be able to take the leave flexibly within 56 weeks of the loss, rather than as a full block.

The CBI, which represents UK businesses, said many employers already provide compassionate leave in these circumstances and it would engage with the government and unions to ensure the details work in practice.

However, the government said "there needs to be a safety net beyond this discretion".

Minister for the Future of Work, Kate Dearden, said: "No one should have to fight for time to grieve.

"These changes back people going through some of the hardest moments of life, whoever they are and wherever they work."

Miscarriage UK described the announcement as "an important step in recognising pregnancy loss as a bereavement".

Chief Executive Vicki Robinson said she hoped it would "provide a baseline for employers to go further", with the charity calling for bereavement leave to be paid.

Bereavement support charity Sue Ryder has also called for the right to paid leave, saying bereavement can have a significant financial impact.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a new law expanding bereavement leave rights to include step, half, adoptive, foster, kinship care relationships, and pregnancy loss, providing meaningful social and workplace support for a broad range of people during difficult times. This legal change has significant positive real-world impact by promoting fairness and mental health support across diverse family structures and circumstances, with clear details on the scope and implementation.
articles.personality_title: UK expands bereavement leave to include more family types and pregnancy loss
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In the UK, people who lose a close family member can take time off work called bereavement leave. Until now, this leave mainly covered close blood relatives.

**What happened** – The government has introduced a new law that broadens who can get bereavement leave. Now, it includes step-relatives, half-relatives, adoptive parents, foster carers, and kinship carers (people who look after children when parents cannot). It also covers pregnancy loss, like miscarriage or unsuccessful IVF, for women and their partners, including intended parents in surrogacy.

**Impact** – This change means many more people will be able to take time off work to grieve without losing their job or income. It recognizes that families come in many forms and that pregnancy loss is a serious loss needing support. The leave can be taken flexibly within a year of the loss, making it easier for people to manage their grief.

**What's next step** – Employers and unions will work with the government to make sure the new rules are fair and practical. Charities are encouraging paid bereavement leave to help people who might face money problems while grieving.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UK now legally supports a wider range of families and pregnancy losses with flexible bereavement leave to help people through difficult times.
articles.personality_title_fr: Royaume-Uni : élargissement du congé de deuil à plus de types de familles et aux pertes de grossesse
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Au Royaume-Uni, les personnes qui perdent un proche peuvent prendre un congé de deuil au travail. Jusqu'à présent, ce congé concernait principalement les proches parents biologiques.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Le gouvernement a adopté une nouvelle loi qui élargit les personnes pouvant bénéficier du congé de deuil. Désormais, il inclut les beaux-parents, demi-parents, parents adoptifs, familles d'accueil et familles d'accueil kinship (qui s'occupent d'enfants lorsque les parents ne peuvent pas). Il couvre aussi la perte de grossesse, comme les fausses couches ou les échecs de FIV, pour les femmes et leurs partenaires, y compris les parents d'intention en gestation pour autrui.

**Impact** – Ce changement permet à beaucoup plus de personnes de prendre un congé pour faire leur deuil sans perdre leur emploi ou revenu. Il reconnaît que les familles sont diverses et que la perte d'une grossesse est une vraie douleur nécessitant du soutien. Le congé peut être pris de façon flexible dans l'année qui suit la perte.

**Prochaine étape** – Les employeurs et syndicats vont travailler avec le gouvernement pour que les règles soient justes et pratiques. Les associations appellent aussi à un congé de deuil payé pour aider ceux qui ont des difficultés financières.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le Royaume-Uni soutient maintenant légalement un plus large éventail de familles et de pertes de grossesse avec un congé de deuil flexible pour accompagner les personnes dans les moments difficiles.
articles.personality_title_es: Reino Unido amplía el permiso por duelo para incluir más tipos de familias y pérdidas de embarazo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En el Reino Unido, las personas que pierden a un familiar cercano pueden tomar un permiso por duelo en el trabajo. Hasta ahora, este permiso cubría principalmente a parientes biológicos cercanos.

**Qué pasó** – El gobierno ha aprobado una nueva ley que amplía quién puede obtener este permiso. Ahora incluye a familiares por afinidad, medios hermanos, padres adoptivos, familias de acogida y cuidadores kinship (personas que cuidan niños cuando los padres no pueden). También cubre la pérdida de embarazo, como abortos espontáneos o fallos en la fertilización in vitro, para mujeres y sus parejas, incluidos padres intencionales en gestación subrogada.

**Impacto** – Este cambio permite que muchas más personas puedan tomarse tiempo libre para el duelo sin perder su trabajo o ingresos. Reconoce que las familias son diversas y que la pérdida de un embarazo es una pérdida seria que necesita apoyo. El permiso se puede usar de forma flexible dentro de un año tras la pérdida.

**Próximo paso** – Los empleadores y sindicatos trabajarán con el gobierno para asegurar que las reglas sean justas y prácticas. Las organizaciones piden que el permiso por duelo sea pagado para ayudar a quienes enfrentan problemas económicos.

**Resumen en una frase** – El Reino Unido ahora apoya legalmente a más tipos de familias y pérdidas de embarazo con un permiso por duelo flexible para ayudar a las personas en momentos difíciles.

articles.title: Six principles for supporting academic freedom in universities
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02932-4Many academics are concerned about threats to independent enquiry in higher education. Here’s how it can be protected while taking legitimate concerns into account.
articles.content:
The university I lead is more than four centuries old and has seen political orders rise and fall. I have not, but I work each day in an institution that remembers those changes — in its archives, statutes and culture of argument. The conditions that make knowledge trustworthy, such as independent peer review, openness about methods and data and the ability to correct earlier work, are changing in ways that reach the core of what a university is for.

How universities came to be — and why they are in trouble now

Those conditions are under pressure in a growing number of countries, and the familiar tools of quiet diplomacy, internal negotiation and isolated warnings no longer keep up with the pace of change. For example, in the past decade, governments in various countries have narrowed the space for independent evidence in different ways.

In the United States, changes to research-funding mechanisms and programme priorities in areas such as climate science and gender research, and the sidelining of environmental and public-health expertise, have shown how quickly political decisions can affect the systems that produce independent evidence (see go.nature.com/4hgg3ym and go.nature.com/4zzmtur). European academies have voiced their concerns in public statements on the pressures facing US science and international collaboration1–2 (see also go.nature.com/4a3pn9s).

In Hungary, a sustained legal campaign around foreign higher-education institutions drove Budapest’s Central European University out of the country to Vienna in 2019. In 2020, the Court of Justice of the European Union found those legal changes incompatible with EU law4,5. The political landscape in Hungary has shifted since then, but the legal tools used and the damage to institutional autonomy and academic freedom remain instructive.

Elsewhere, grant language is being rewritten to steer funding priorities towards favoured themes such as economic competitiveness, innovation and national security. Access to public data in sensitive areas such as climate and health is being reduced, and researchers are adapting proposals accordingly, sometimes by avoiding or adding certain topics or terms to maximize their chances in the next funding round.

The details differ, yet the pattern is familiar to many of us who work in universities. One question keeps returning: when governments or funders intervene in universities, do they strengthen or weaken the checks that make knowledge trustworthy?

Others have warned about these threats to independent enquiry already1,2,6. Here, I try to turn these concerns into a set of principles that can guide real decisions in the messy situations academics face. They can be used as a test for any measure that affects universities, and apply to governments, funders and university leaders alike.

They are written for people who have to decide, often under time pressure, where legitimate steering of a publicly funded system ends and interference with independent knowledge begins. They concern both the freedom of academics to pursue questions wherever the evidence leads, and the ability of universities to protect that work from undue influence. These are distinct but connected responsibilities, because pressures on one often weaken the other.

The first three principles set out why independent enquiry must be protected and how that protection is anchored in the university’s core task. The last three show when that protection has to be weighed against other legitimate concerns.

Ground academic freedom in the duty to produce reliable knowledge

Universities have a responsibility to produce reliable knowledge of lasting public value — including for people who will never set foot in a lecture hall — and to teach students how to think using that knowledge. Academic freedom is the working condition that makes this possible.

I learnt this from supervisors who allowed me to ask awkward questions and from students who pushed back in seminars. We are answerable first for the quality and integrity of the knowledge we produce and teach. Academic freedom is one of the tools that allow us to live up to that responsibility.

Discussions about academic freedom often start with rights and only later bring in responsibility as a limit. I prefer to reverse that order: universities are first accountable for the quality of the knowledge they create and pass on, and academic freedom and institutional autonomy are the conditions in which to do this well.

Research that bends towards political or commercial pressure carries that pressure into the questions that are asked, the methods that are chosen and the outcomes that are presented7,8. Teaching that pushes political instructions to the fore trains students to adapt their thinking to approved answers instead of testing arguments against disciplinary standards (see go.nature.com/4a3pn9s).

Teaching students how to use reliable knowledge to inform their thinking is a university’s core task.Credit: AzmanJaka/Getty

External directives that decide in advance which questions might be asked or which answers are acceptable reduce the space to question assumptions and to correct mistakes. When the people who produce and teach knowledge cannot work independently, they gradually lose the ability to correct each other and to correct those in power.

Quality is often the main reason given for defending academic freedom. It is also the main language used to justify limiting it. Some governments frame measures that reduce universities’ capacity for independent enquiry in terms of quality, integrity, balance or public safety, presenting these interventions as ways to protect academic standards. What matters is how knowledge is produced in practice, whether others can see and test what has been done and whether it proves reliable over decades.

Measures that genuinely improve knowledge make methods and results easier to check and to challenge. However, changing grant calls to favour certain answers, screening researchers for their views or taking uncomfortable data offline weakens that scrutiny and minimizes what can be known from work that has already been done. The test for any such measure is whether it strengthens independent scrutiny, and with it the university’s ability to meet its responsibility to society.

Protect questions that have value that cannot be shown in advance

Curiosity-driven research often leads to applications that no one can predict. If researchers limit in advance which questions they will pursue, they also limit the futures that science can open up.

There are various examples of such applications that were initially unpredictable. Work on how bacteria defend themselves against viruses became CRISPR gene editing, now the basis of a therapy for sickle-cell disease. Research in linguistics and digital humanities helped to build translation tools and search systems. Long-term epidemiological cohort studies underpin public-health guidance on smoking, diet, workplace safety and environmental exposure. Decades of work on messenger RNA and lipid-nanoparticle delivery became the platform for COVID-19 vaccines when the world needed them. None of these lines of work would have scored highly for societal relevance at the start.

Key US science panels are being axed — and others are becoming less open

Research should speak to societal challenges, but funding systems also need to preserve room for questions with a value that cannot yet be specified. Narrowly defined relevance criteria tend to reward safe, incremental projects and push researchers towards low-risk enquiry. Free enquiry matters precisely because scientists do not know in advance which questions will turn out to be important.

A government that wants to base policy on robust knowledge depends on a research system that can generate and test that knowledge independently. Cutting public investment in fundamental research might reduce spending today, but it shifts the cost into the future — through missed treatments, weaker prevention, lost innovation and a reduced capacity to respond when the next crisis arrives. The test is whether a measure unduly narrows the range of questions that can still be asked.

Treat universities as democratic infrastructure

Universities disperse power in practice by training professionals who can question official decisions, by producing analyses that can contradict government or corporate claims and by placing independent expertise inside courts of law, in the media and in public debate. Together with the executive, legislative and judicial branches, and with a free press and civil society, universities form a pillar of a society that is built on democracy, human rights and the rule of law. When that wider structure is weakened, universities are usually affected as well.

Hungary shows how this can unfold. Between 2017 and 2019, Viktor Orbán’s government reduced the independence of universities and research institutes by transferring control of research funding from the national academy of sciences to a new research network. The network’s board is chaired by a government-appointed minister’s nominee. The government used higher-education law to force the Central European University abroad, and brought law courts, the press and civil society under tighter political control through parallel legislative changes4.

Elsewhere, earmarked funding, new laws on cooperation, politicized appointments to governing boards and a steady public attack on expertise point in a similar direction. Examples of such trends are described in global and EU-wide academic freedom monitors and national reports9–11.

It does not take dramatic events abroad to damage academic freedom. In my own country, the Netherlands, the national academy warned in 2025 that large budget cuts increase the pressure to shift from independent to commissioned research, and that a proposed screening law on knowledge security would limit researchers’ freedom to choose their collaboration partners. It also documented self-censorship after researchers were intimidated in public debates12. Rectors of Dutch universities warned in the same year of a growing political tendency to steer the content of scientific debate and teaching (see go.nature.com/3v3ktjj).

Institutional autonomy means being accountable to the public for the quality and integrity of knowledge, rather than to a government for whether it finds the conclusions politically acceptable. Rules and accountability frameworks are not in themselves a problem. Many exist to protect people, ensure workplace safety or guard public funds. A problem arises when their combined effect, including funding conditions, reporting requirements and rules on cooperation, shifts the centre of control from the university to the ministry. One form of accountability strengthens independent knowledge; the other replaces it with political acceptability.

Hold security and openness as a single responsibility

The case for academic freedom is linked to that for research security. The risks of espionage, loss of intellectual property and harmful use of sensitive knowledge are real, and universities cannot ignore them.

At the same time, security measures that are designed without attention to academic freedom can unintentionally narrow independent enquiry and place a great deal of control in the hands of those who manage access to data, infrastructure and international collaboration.
articles.reasoning: The article addresses the protection of academic freedom in universities, highlighting its critical role in producing reliable knowledge and supporting democratic society. It discusses real-world challenges and proposes principles to safeguard independent enquiry, which has broad societal significance and positive impact on education, research integrity, and democratic infrastructure.

articles.title: ‘We are not powerless’: UN chief urges world leaders to invest in peace
articles.summary: In a world facing rising conflicts, violence and divisions that are causing great suffering for millions of people, the UN chief on Monday called on world leaders and citizens to invest more in peace.
articles.content:
“Achieving peace is not something that just happens,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in a message for Monday’s International Day of Peace. “It is a shared and decisive choice to invest in a better future.”

Invest in peace is this year’s theme, echoing the founding principles of the UN, built amid the ashes of the Second World War.

As world leaders gather at UN Headquarters for the annual High-Level Week, Mr. Guterres called on them to strengthen diplomacy, dialogue, mediation and peacekeeping operations as essential means of preventing and resolving conflicts.

Indeed, peace – a vital resource for human development – remains elusive in many parts of the world as conflicts increase in scale and complexity, he said.

Watch the UN chief’s full message here:

‘We must talk to one another’

At an event marking the day at the UN’s hub in Nairobi, Kenya, young people weighed in.

Pointing to “something that does not help in maintaining peace”, Benedict Wambuya, an agriculture and technology student at Jomo Kenyatta University, reflected on recent deadly crackdowns at home, when young people felt their rights were being violated by State authorities.

“As young people, we are hardly ever involved in peace discussions around the world,” he said. “We are not participating enough in maintaining peace around the world. We should seek to understand our leaders, come together, work together and maintain peace.”

Benedict Kioko, a Kenyatta University student, agreed.

“For peace to last, there must be mutual understanding,” he said. “We must talk to one another so that we can reach an understanding. Often, peace has been disrupted because there has been a lack of dialogue or understanding between two different sides.”

Festus Musau, a student at the Technical University of Kenya, said “everything is connected to peace.”

“For peace to thrive in a country,” he said, “it must begin with every individual.”

Crossing the border

Many societies around the world face violence and division while conflicts spill across national borders.

In the face of this, finding solutions has been challenging, with international solidarity weakening, the UN Secretary-General said.

Lasting peace needs to be built through inclusive societies, sustainable development and respect for human rights.

Watch today's UN-hosted intergenerational Peace Circle:

‘We are not powerless’

“Around the world, people are showing that we are not powerless,” he said. “Volunteers, advocates, civil society leaders, peacekeepers and peacemakers are bridging divides, uniting communities, and pushing for dialogue. Action by action, they are building peace from the ground up.”

These grassroots efforts show that peace can only be achieved if deliberate decisions are taken to invest in a better future, he said.

Tweet URL

How does the UN invest in peace?

The UN is mandated by its 193 Member States to help nations prevent, resolve and recover from conflict.

From diplomacy and peacekeeping missions to working with communities to foster peace, efforts began right at the UN’s inception.

Here are some examples:

Peacekeeping and peacebuilding: Since 1948, the UN Security Council has deployed more than 70 missions around the world. Currently, 11 peacekeeping missions are operating. Learn more about the broad work of the UN Department of Peacekeeping and Peacebuilding here.

Peace Circle: On Monday, the UN Hear Us. Act Now for a Peaceful World campaign brings young voices and contributions in to a forthcoming independent progress study on how young people contribute to peace, with a Peace Circle event.

Peaceful world activation: From 14 to 26 September (International Day for the Elimination of Nuclear Weapons), the UN’s ActNow initiative is helping connect audiences with information and opportunities to take action, including via its mobile app partner, Through A World.

But, can the UN stop a war? Watch our explainer:

Learn more about UN peace efforts here.

articles.personality_title_es: El jefe de la ONU insta a los líderes a invertir en la paz para un futuro más seguro
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El mundo enfrenta más conflictos y violencia que causan sufrimiento a millones de personas. La Organización de las Naciones Unidas (ONU) se creó después de la Segunda Guerra Mundial para promover la paz y evitar guerras.

**Qué pasó** – En el Día Internacional de la Paz, el secretario general de la ONU, António Guterres, pidió a los líderes mundiales y a todas las personas invertir más en la paz. Habló sobre la necesidad de diplomacia, diálogo y misiones de mantenimiento de la paz para detener los conflictos. Jóvenes en Kenia también compartieron que la paz comienza con entenderse y hablar.

**Impacto** – Esta llamada es importante porque la paz no ocurre por sí sola; necesita decisiones activas y trabajo de gobiernos y comunidades. La ONU ha enviado misiones de paz desde 1948, mostrando que los esfuerzos por la paz ocurren en altos niveles y en la gente común. Las voces jóvenes recuerdan que la paz duradera necesita la participación de todos.

**Próximo paso** – La ONU y sus países miembros continuarán apoyando misiones de paz y fomentando más diálogo y cooperación. Campañas como ActNow y Peace Circle ayudarán a las personas a aprender cómo contribuir a la paz en sus comunidades.

**Frase clave** – El jefe de la ONU pide a todos elegir la paz trabajando juntos con diálogo, cascos azules y acciones comunitarias para construir un mundo más seguro.

articles.title: Vet prescription fees capped under rule changes
articles.summary: Vets must also tell clients if cheaper medicine is available online as part of the rule updates which surgeries have the coming months to bring in.
articles.content:
Written prescription fees from vets will be capped at £21 as part of a raft of changes that practices will be legally required to bring in over the coming months.

Vets must also tell clients if cheaper medicine is available online, write price estimates ahead of treatment, and publish price lists for services as part of the rule updates.

The official competition watchdog has brought the measures into force after its investigation into the sector found prices had been rising at nearly twice the rate of inflation.

However, critics say the measures will hit independent vets hardest and will benefit the six firms that own more than two-thirds of practices.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) made its remedies for the sector legally binding as of Tuesday and vets have up to 12 months to bring all the changes in.

As well as capping prescription fees, other changes include:

Vet practices must publish a "comprehensive" price list for standard services – including consultations, common procedures, and cremation options

A written estimate must be provided in advance for any treatment expected to cost £500 or more, including aftercare costs, plus an itemised bill. Emergencies are the only exception to this

Vet businesses must make clear whether they are part of a group or an independent business

To help pet owners compare local practices, price and ownership information will be made available through the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons' "Find a Vet" service, which will share the data with third-party comparison sites.

The timelines for when vets need to bring in the fixes depends on the exact regulation and the group's size. The CMA sets it out here., external

"The changes that are being required are changes that will help inform pet owners about prices," said CMA panel chair Martin Coleman.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a regulatory change capping veterinary prescription fees and increasing price transparency, which benefits pet owners by making veterinary care more affordable and transparent. This has broad, tangible positive impact on consumers and pet welfare, addressing a sector-wide issue of rising costs. The article provides detailed context about the measures and their implementation timeline, indicating substantive policy change.
articles.personality_title: New rules cap vet prescription fees and improve price transparency
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Vet prices have been rising faster than the cost of living, making it harder for pet owners to afford care. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) investigated and found that prices were increasing too quickly.

**What happened** – Starting now, vets must limit prescription fees to £21. They also have to tell pet owners if cheaper medicines are available online, provide price estimates before treatment costing £500 or more, and publish clear price lists for common services. These rules must be fully in place within a year.

**Impact** – These changes help pet owners by making vet costs clearer and more affordable. Knowing prices in advance and having access to cheaper medicine options online means people can better plan for their pet’s care. The new rules also allow easier price comparison between vets.

**What's next step** – Vets will update their pricing and information systems over the next 12 months. The Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons will share this data to help pet owners find and compare local vets. This may encourage fairer prices and better service.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New government rules limit vet prescription fees and require clear pricing to help pet owners afford and understand the cost of care.
articles.personality_title_fr: Nouvelles règles plafonnent les frais de prescription vétérinaire et améliorent la transparence des prix
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les prix des soins vétérinaires ont augmenté plus vite que le coût de la vie, rendant les soins plus difficiles à payer pour les propriétaires d’animaux. L’Autorité de la concurrence du Royaume-Uni (CMA) a enquêté et constaté une hausse trop rapide des prix.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Désormais, les vétérinaires doivent limiter les frais de prescription à 21 £. Ils doivent aussi informer les propriétaires si des médicaments moins chers sont disponibles en ligne, fournir des devis pour les traitements coûtant 500 £ ou plus, et publier des listes de prix claires pour les services courants. Ces règles doivent être appliquées dans l’année.

**Impact** – Ces changements aident les propriétaires d’animaux en rendant les coûts vétérinaires plus clairs et abordables. Connaître les prix à l’avance et avoir accès à des médicaments moins chers en ligne permet de mieux préparer les soins. Les règles facilitent aussi la comparaison des prix entre vétérinaires.

**Prochaine étape** – Les vétérinaires vont mettre à jour leurs systèmes de tarification et d’information dans les 12 mois. Le Collège royal des chirurgiens vétérinaires partagera ces données pour aider à trouver et comparer les vétérinaires locaux. Cela pourrait encourager des prix plus justes et un meilleur service.

**Une phrase clé** – De nouvelles règles limitent les frais de prescription vétérinaire et imposent la transparence des prix pour aider les propriétaires à mieux comprendre et payer les soins.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevas reglas limitan las tarifas de prescripción veterinaria y mejoran la transparencia de precios
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los precios de los veterinarios han estado subiendo más rápido que el costo de vida, dificultando que los dueños de mascotas paguen por los cuidados. La Autoridad de Competencia y Mercados del Reino Unido (CMA) investigó y encontró aumentos demasiado rápidos.

**Qué pasó** – Ahora, los veterinarios deben limitar las tarifas de prescripción a £21. También deben informar a los dueños si hay medicinas más baratas en línea, dar presupuestos para tratamientos que cuesten £500 o más, y publicar listas claras de precios para servicios comunes. Estas reglas deben estar en vigor dentro de un año.

**Impacto** – Estos cambios ayudan a los dueños de mascotas al hacer los costos veterinarios más claros y accesibles. Saber los precios antes y tener opciones más baratas en línea permite planificar mejor los cuidados. Las reglas también facilitan comparar precios entre veterinarios.

**Próximo paso** – Los veterinarios actualizarán sus sistemas de precios e información en los próximos 12 meses. El Colegio Real de Cirujanos Veterinarios compartirá estos datos para ayudar a encontrar y comparar veterinarios locales. Esto podría promover precios más justos y mejor servicio.

**Una frase para recordar** – Nuevas reglas limitan las tarifas de prescripción veterinaria y exigen transparencia en los precios para ayudar a los dueños a entender y pagar mejor los cuidados.
